text: Book II of the *Republic* contains two arguments, and later readers have often treated them separately. The first builds a city from scratch. Socrates offers it less as political theory than as a way of seeing the soul at a larger scale: the city is the person magnified, the same letters written large (368d–369a). The second sets rules for what may be said about the gods (379a ff.), and here Plato was entering a quarrel already some two hundred years old. Homer and Hesiod were the closest thing Greece had to scripture, and their gods lied, lusted, fought their own kin, and handed out good and evil from two jars (*Iliad* 24.527–533). The philosopher Xenophanes had mocked those portraits in the sixth century BCE. In 399 BCE an Athenian jury condemned Socrates on charges of impiety and of corrupting the young. Plato's answer is to make the founders of his city theologians before they are lawgivers. They settle what a god must be before they settle what children may hear. The whole construction also rests on a founding premise, that a city is a remedy for human neediness. Aristotle later disputed it. For him the city was something natural to human beings.
